short.title_plain: Bronze Gear in Han Tomb Challenges Ancient Tech
short.hook: A 2,000-year-old bronze gear was found in Emperor Wen's tomb.
script: A 2,000-year-old bronze gear was found in Emperor Wen's tomb.
It has 36 evenly spaced teeth and a smooth, precisely machined surface.
Experts believe it resembles a modern gear but its function remains unknown.
It may have been part of a carriage or mechanical device, but no matching parts were found.
Wear marks and alloy analysis suggest advanced craftsmanship, not a full mechanical system.
Some statues show shackles, hinting at forced labor in imperial projects.
Did ancient China build mechanical systems—or just master precision toolmaking?
Tap the link below for the full case file.
short.description:
A bronze gear with 36 evenly spaced teeth was discovered in the tomb of Emperor Wen of Han at Ba Ling, Shaanxi province. The gear shows high precision in machining, suggesting advanced metalworking skills. However, its function remains undetermined; it may have been used for locking or positioning, not as part of a transmission system. Experts emphasize that the gear does not prove the existence of complex mechanical technology in ancient China. Source: Vietnam.vn, https://www.vietnam.vn/en/bat-ngo-banh-rang-dong-tinh-xao-trong-lang-mo-han-van-de
